topics.title: Need for adjustments and the treatment of closing stock

learn.hook: The trial balance is a rough draft. Unpaid March salaries, next year's insurance paid today and unsold stock are all missing or misplaced. Adjustments turn the draft into a true picture.
points: Adjustments make the final accounts follow the accrual and matching concepts: every income and expense of the year, and only of the year, is included.

Golden rule: an item given INSIDE the trial balance appears at ONE place in the final accounts; an adjustment given OUTSIDE the trial balance appears at TWO places (double effect), e.g. P&L and balance sheet.
Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower (conservatism).
Closing stock given outside the trial balance: credit side of the trading account and current asset in the balance sheet.
Closing stock given inside the trial balance (with adjusted purchases, i.e. purchases already reduced by closing stock): shown only in the balance sheet, not in the trading account.

example.q: Closing stock: cost ₹90,000, net realisable value ₹84,000; given outside the trial balance. Show its treatment.
steps: Value at the lower: ₹84,000.
Trading account credit side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
Balance sheet assets side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
example.answer: ₹84,000 on the credit of the trading account and as a current asset in the balance sheet.

learn.reallife: Pharmacies in India must value near-expiry medicines below cost if they will fetch less; lower of cost or net realisable value keeps profits honest.

Answer: On the credit side of the trading account and as an asset in the balance sheet
quiz.mistake: Shows the adjustment at only one place

quiz.q: Closing stock: cost ₹1,20,000, NRV ₹1,35,000. At what value is it taken?
quiz.explain: Lower of cost and NRV.

options: On the credit side of the trading account and in the balance sheet
Only on the credit side of the trading account
Only in the balance sheet
On the debit side of the P&L account
quiz.explain: Purchases are already adjusted for closing stock.
steps: 'Adjusted purchases' are already reduced by closing stock.
Showing closing stock in trading again would count it twice.
So closing stock appears only in the balance sheet.
Answer: Only in the balance sheet

quiz.q: Why are adjustments made before preparing final accounts?
options: To make the trial balance agree
To reduce tax illegally
To avoid preparing a balance sheet
To include all incomes and expenses of the period, following accrual and matching
quiz.explain: Adjustments bring the accounts to the accrual basis.
steps: Accrual and matching need every income and expense of the year, and only of the year.
Adjustments bring outstanding, prepaid and similar items into the accounts.
So adjustments include all incomes and expenses of the period.
Answer: To include all incomes and expenses of the period, following accrual and matching

quiz.q: An item appearing in the trial balance is shown in the final accounts at
options: One place
Two places
Three places
No place
quiz.explain: Its double entry is already done in the ledger.
steps: An item inside the trial balance already has its double entry in the ledger.

Answer: One place

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.
Reason (R): The conservatism concept requires anticipating no profit but providing for all possible losses.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Valuing at the lower figure avoids recording unrealised profit and provides for expected loss.
steps: A: closing stock is valued at lower of cost and NRV. True.
R: conservatism means anticipating no profit and providing for all losses. True.
Taking the lower value follows exactly that rule, so R explains A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Links stock valuation with consistency only

quiz.q: Net sales ₹5,00,000; opening stock ₹60,000; purchases ₹3,50,000; closing stock (outside the trial balance) cost ₹80,000, NRV ₹70,000. Gross profit?
quiz.explain: Closing stock is taken at ₹70,000.

quiz.q: Case: Trial balance shows adjusted purchases ₹2,80,000 and closing stock ₹40,000; sales ₹4,00,000; no opening stock or direct expenses in the trading account. Gross profit?

revise.summary: Adjustments bring the final accounts onto the accrual and matching basis. A trial balance item appears once; an adjustment outside it appears twice. Closing stock is valued at lower of cost and NRV.

learn.hook: March salary is paid on 7 April. Next year's insurance is paid in January. Both payments land in the wrong year unless we adjust them.
points: Outstanding expense: incurred during the year but not yet paid. Adjusting entry: Dr Expense / Cr Outstanding Expense.
Treatment: add to the expense in the P&L (or trading) account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance for a period beyond the year. Adjusting entry: Dr Prepaid Expense / Cr Expense.
Treatment: deduct from the expense in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Outstanding wages go to the trading account (wages are direct); outstanding salaries, rent and so on go to the P&L account.

example.q: Rent paid during 2025-26 is ₹55,000 (11 months). Monthly rent ₹5,000. Insurance paid ₹12,000 on 1 October 2025 for one year. Show the adjustments.
steps: Rent outstanding = 1 month = ₹5,000; P&L rent = 55,000 + 5,000 = ₹60,000; liability ₹5,000.
Insurance: October to March = 6 months used; prepaid = 6/12 × 12,000 = ₹6,000.
P&L insurance = 12,000 − 6,000 = ₹6,000; current asset ₹6,000.

learn.reallife: Indian companies show 'outstanding expenses' under other current liabilities and 'prepaid expenses' under other current assets in their Schedule III balance sheets.

topics.title: Accrued income and income received in advance

learn.hook: Your fixed deposit earned interest in March, but the bank credits it in April. You've earned it already. And a tenant who pays April's rent in March? You haven't earned that yet.
points: Accrued income: earned during the year but not yet received, e.g. interest accrued on investments, commission earned not received.
Adjusting entry: Dr Accrued Income / Cr Income. Treatment: add to the income in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Income received in advance (unearned income): received during the year for a service to be given next year, e.g. rent received in advance.
Adjusting entry: Dr Income / Cr Income Received in Advance. Treatment: deduct from the income in the P&L account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.

example.q: Investments ₹2,00,000 at 9% p.a.; interest received during the year ₹12,000. Rent received ₹60,000 includes ₹10,000 for the next year. Show the treatment.
steps: P&L: interest ₹18,000; balance sheet: accrued interest ₹6,000 (current asset).
Rent: P&L 60,000 − 10,000 = ₹50,000; balance sheet: rent received in advance ₹10,000 (current liability).
example.answer: Interest ₹18,000 (accrued ₹6,000 asset); rent ₹50,000 (₹10,000 advance as liability).

learn.reallife: Coaching institutes in India often collect a full year's fees upfront; at the financial year-end, fees for months not yet taught are income received in advance.

topics.title: Depreciation and bad debts as adjustments

learn.hook: A furniture showroom's balance sheet should not show three-year-old furniture at its original price, nor debtors who have vanished. Two adjustments fix that.
points: Depreciation adjustment: debit P&L account with depreciation; deduct it from the asset in the balance sheet.
If an asset is added during the year, depreciation on the addition is charged only for the months used (unless told otherwise).
Bad debts given inside the trial balance: debited to P&L only (debtors are already reduced).
Further bad debts given as an adjustment: add to bad debts in P&L, and deduct from debtors in the balance sheet.
Bad debts recovered (an amount written off earlier, now received) is credited to P&L as an income.

example.q: Machinery ₹3,00,000 (including ₹60,000 bought on 1 October 2025). Depreciation 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March 2026. Debtors ₹1,20,000; bad debts in trial balance ₹3,000; further bad debts ₹2,000. Show the treatment.
steps: Depreciation on ₹2,40,000 for 12 months = ₹24,000; on ₹60,000 for 6 months = ₹3,000; total ₹27,000.
P&L debit: depreciation ₹27,000; balance sheet: machinery 3,00,000 − 27,000 = ₹2,73,000.
Bad debts in P&L = 3,000 + 2,000 = ₹5,000; debtors in balance sheet = 1,20,000 − 2,000 = ₹1,18,000.

learn.reallife: Small distributors of FMCG products in towns like Nagpur write off unpaid dues of retailers who shut shop, and adjust their debtors list at the year-end.

topics.title: Provision for doubtful debts and provision for discount on debtors

learn.hook: First remove the debtors who won't pay at all, then the ones who might not, and finally the discount the good ones will take for paying early. The order matters.
points: Provision for doubtful debts (PDD) is calculated as a percentage of debtors after deducting further bad debts.
P&L charge = Bad debts (trial balance) + Further bad debts + New PDD − Old PDD. If the result is negative, the surplus is credited to P&L.
Balance sheet: Debtors − Further bad debts − New PDD.
Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts and the new PDD (only good debtors receive discount).
It is debited to P&L (less any old provision for discount) and deducted from debtors in the balance sheet.

example.q: Debtors ₹1,00,000; further bad debts ₹4,000; PDD 5%; provision for discount 2%. Old PDD ₹3,000; bad debts in TB ₹1,000. Find the P&L charges and net debtors.
steps: Debtors after bad debts = ₹96,000; new PDD = 5% = ₹4,800.
example.answer: P&L: ₹6,800 for bad and doubtful debts and ₹1,824 for discount; net debtors ₹89,376.

learn.reallife: Wholesale traders in Mumbai's Crawford Market often allow a small discount for prompt payment, so they provide for it at year-end on their good debtors.

topics.title: Interest on capital and interest on drawings

learn.hook: A proprietor who invests ₹10 lakh could have earned interest in a bank. Charging interest on capital shows whether the business earns more than that bank deposit would have.
points: Interest on capital: an expense of the business, debited to P&L; added to the owner's capital in the balance sheet. Entry: Dr Interest on Capital / Cr Capital.
Interest on drawings: an income of the business, credited to P&L; deducted from capital in the balance sheet (directly or through drawings). Entry: Dr Drawings (or Capital) / Cr Interest on Drawings.
Interest on capital = Capital × Rate × Time. If capital is added during the year, interest on the addition runs from the date of addition.
Interest on drawings = Drawings × Rate × Period for which the money was withdrawn.
These adjustments do not change the owner's final capital in total; they show the true earnings of the business.

example.q: Capital ₹5,00,000 on 1 April 2025; interest on capital 8% p.a. Drawings ₹40,000 withdrawn on 1 October 2025; interest on drawings 6% p.a. Year ends 31 March 2026.
steps: Interest on capital = 5,00,000 × 8% = ₹40,000 (debit P&L; add to capital).
Interest on drawings = 40,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,200 (credit P&L; deduct from capital).
example.answer: Interest on capital ₹40,000; interest on drawings ₹1,200.

topics.title: Other adjustments: abnormal loss, goods withdrawn, samples, unrecorded items

learn.hook: A godown fire, a proprietor taking goods home and boxes given away as samples all reduce the goods available for sale. Each needs a careful two-place treatment.
points: Abnormal loss of goods (fire, theft, flood) given as an adjustment: credit the trading account with the full cost of goods lost; debit P&L with the loss not covered by insurance; show the insurance claim admitted as a current asset.
Goods withdrawn by the proprietor (adjustment): deduct from purchases in the trading account (at cost) and add to drawings (deducted from capital).
Goods distributed as free samples (adjustment): deduct from purchases and debit advertisement in P&L.
Unrecorded credit sales: add to sales and to debtors. Unrecorded credit purchases (goods included in stock): add to purchases and to creditors.
Goods sent on approval and wrongly recorded as sales, not yet approved: reduce sales and debtors by the sale price, and include them in closing stock at cost.

example.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 destroyed by fire; insurance claim admitted ₹30,000 (adjustment). Show the treatment.
steps: Trading account credit: Loss by fire (goods destroyed) ₹50,000.
P&L debit: loss not covered = 50,000 − 30,000 = ₹20,000.
Balance sheet assets: insurance claim receivable ₹30,000.
example.answer: Trading Cr ₹50,000; P&L Dr ₹20,000; balance sheet asset ₹30,000.

learn.hook: This is the big question of the Class 11 exam: a trial balance with six or seven adjustments. Work methodically, one adjustment at a time, and the balance sheet will tally.
points: Work in order: closing stock; outstanding and prepaid expenses; accrued and advance incomes; depreciation; bad debts and provisions; manager's commission; interest on capital and drawings.
